questions.stem: What does a magnetic survey measure when exploring for minerals?
options: The concentration of metals in samples of soil and stream mud
Local variations in the strength of the Earth's magnetic field
The time taken for sound waves to reflect back from buried rock layers
Small differences in the pull of gravity from place to place
questions.explanation: A magnetometer, often towed by an aircraft, records how the strength of the magnetic field varies. Rocks rich in magnetic minerals such as magnetite produce anomalies. Reflected sound waves are the basis of seismic surveys.

questions.stem: An airborne magnetic survey shows a strong, isolated anomaly beneath thick sand cover. Which buried body is most likely to cause it?
options: A body of rock rich in magnetite
A thick layer of pure quartz sand
A large body of rock salt
A coal seam full of methane
questions.explanation: Magnetite is strongly magnetic, so a magnetite-rich body raises the local field. Quartz, salt and coal are essentially non-magnetic, so they do not produce strong magnetic highs.

questions.stem: How does an electromagnetic (EM) survey detect a buried body of massive sulfide ore?
options: A gravimeter detects the greater density of the sulfide ore than the host rock
Geophones detect sound waves that reflect off the upper surface of the ore body
A transmitted field induces currents in the conductive ore, which a receiver detects
A magnetometer detects the natural magnetism of every one of the sulfide minerals in the ore
questions.explanation: An EM system sends a changing magnetic field into the ground. Good electrical conductors such as massive sulfides carry induced currents, which create a secondary field that the receiver measures. Many sulfides are not strongly magnetic, so a magnetometer alone may miss them.

questions.stem: An EM survey finds a strong conductor, but drilling hits graphite-rich shale with no ore. Why can this happen?
options: Graphite also conducts electricity, so it gives a similar EM response
Graphite is magnetic, so it distorts the field from the transmitter
Graphite is denser than sulfides, so it masks the response of the ore
Graphite absorbs all the transmitted signal, so the survey is not valid
questions.explanation: EM surveys respond to electrical conductivity, not to metal content. Graphite and saline groundwater are good conductors too, so an anomaly is a target to be tested by drilling, not proof of ore.

questions.stem: In a stream sediment survey, geologists sample mud from many creeks in a catchment. What are they looking for?
options: Fossils in the mud that show the age of the rocks upstream
Changes in each creek's flow rate that show where the major faults lie
Pebbles of granite that show where volcanoes once erupted
Higher than normal levels of metals that point to a source upstream
questions.explanation: Weathering releases metals from an ore body, and creeks carry them downstream in sediment. Sampling many creeks and following rising metal levels upstream narrows down where the source lies.

questions.stem: Copper values in creek sediment are low in creeks A and B, high in creek C below a junction, and highest in creek D, a tributary of C. Where should soil sampling focus next?
options: The floodplain far downstream of the junction
Equally across all four catchments at random
The catchment of creek D, upstream of the junction
The catchment of creek A, where values are lowest
questions.explanation: Metal levels rise towards the source, so the highest values in tributary D point to its catchment. Low values in A and B suggest no source there, and sampling downstream would move away from the source.

questions.stem: Soil samples on a grid show copper concentrations that rise gradually towards one point, forming a broad zone of raised values. What is this zone called?
options: A gravity low above a body of rock salt
A seismic reflector at a change of rock type
A geochemical halo around a buried ore body
A magnetic anomaly over a magnetite body
questions.explanation: Metals spread from an ore body into the surrounding rock and soil, forming a halo of raised values that is larger than the deposit itself and so easier to find. Magnetic, gravity and seismic anomalies are geophysical, not chemical.

questions.stem: Why is drilling needed even after geophysical and geochemical surveys have found a target?
options: Drilling is the only exploration method that causes no environmental impact
Only drilling recovers samples that confirm the grade and extent of the ore
Only drilling can measure the strength of the Earth's magnetic field
Drilling is cheaper than surveys, so it is used to save money
questions.explanation: Surveys are indirect: they show anomalies that might be ore. Drill samples are direct evidence of the rock, so assays of them confirm the grade, thickness and extent of a deposit. Drilling is expensive and does have impacts, such as tracks and drill pads.

questions.stem: A company must decide whether a deposit is worth mining and how its ore body is faulted. Why would it choose diamond drilling over cheaper reverse circulation drilling?
options: Diamond drilling uses no water or drilling fluid, so it has no impact at all
Diamond drilling recovers solid core that shows rock structure and texture
Diamond drilling recovers rock chips that are easier to assay than core
Diamond drilling reaches only shallow depths, so it is quicker and safer
questions.explanation: Diamond drilling cuts an intact cylinder of core, which preserves textures, veins, faults and contacts, so geologists can map the ore body in detail. Reverse circulation drilling returns broken chips, which are cheaper to collect but lose the structure.

questions.stem: In a seismic survey for petroleum, what do the geophones or hydrophones record?
options: Natural radiation given off by the rocks exposed at the surface
Sound waves reflected from boundaries between rock layers
Changes in the pull of gravity caused by buried rocks
Electric currents induced in buried conductive rocks
questions.explanation: A source such as a vibrator truck on land or an air gun at sea sends sound waves down. Part of the energy reflects at each boundary between layers, and the arrival times are used to map the layers beneath the surface.

questions.stem: Why are seismic surveys the main tool for finding petroleum traps?
options: They detect oil directly, because oil reflects sound more strongly than rock
They measure the temperature of buried rocks to find the oil window
They show the magnetism of the source rock in which the oil formed
They map the shape of buried layers, revealing folds, faults and salt domes
questions.explanation: Seismic sections show the geometry of rock layers, so geologists can find structures such as anticlines, faults and salt domes that could trap oil. A trap may still be empty, so only drilling confirms petroleum.

questions.stem: A seismic reflection takes 2.0 s to travel down to a rock boundary and back up. If sound travels at an average 3000 m/s in these rocks, how deep is the boundary?
questions.explanation: The 2.0 s is the two-way time, so the wave took 1.0 s to reach the boundary. Depth = 3000 m/s x 1.0 s = 3000 m. Using the full 2.0 s gives 6000 m, the total path length rather than the depth.

questions.stem: A gravity survey over a sedimentary basin shows a circular area where gravity is slightly lower than its surroundings. Which buried structure could explain this and interest a petroleum explorer?
options: A granite intrusion, because granite is denser than sedimentary rock
A basalt lava flow, because basalt is less dense than sandstone
A salt dome, because salt is less dense than the rocks around it
A body of iron ore, because it is denser than the rocks around it
questions.explanation: Gravity is slightly lower over rock that is less dense than its surroundings. Rock salt is less dense than most buried sediments, so a salt dome gives a gravity low, and salt domes can form petroleum traps. Iron ore and basalt are dense and would give gravity highs.

questions.stem: Olympic Dam in South Australia was found by drilling where a gravity high and a magnetic high coincided beneath thick cover. Why was the combination a stronger target than either alone?
options: A gravity high alone always shows ore, so the magnetic data added no value
Magnetic highs show copper directly, so the gravity data located the depth
Dense, magnetic iron-oxide-rich rock explains both, which few other rocks do
The two surveys measure the same property, so the result was confirmed twice
questions.explanation: Gravity and magnetic surveys measure different properties: density and magnetism. A body that is both dense and magnetic, such as rock rich in iron oxides, narrows the possible causes. Neither anomaly shows copper directly, which is why the target had to be drilled.

questions.stem: A geologist finds a rusty, porous, iron-oxide-rich rock cap on a hill. Why might this lead to drilling?
options: It may be a gossan, the weathered top of a sulfide ore body
It may be a placer deposit of gold washed down from the hill
It may be a coal seam that has been burnt by a bushfire
It may be a salt dome that has risen through the sediments
questions.explanation: When sulfide minerals weather near the surface, the metals are leached and iron oxides are left behind as a gossan. Gossans have led prospectors to many buried sulfide deposits.

questions.stem: Plants growing over a buried metal deposit are stunted, or a metal-tolerant species dominates there. What does this show?
options: A resource heats the soil above it, so only heat-tolerant plants survive
A resource blocks rainfall from reaching the soil above the deposit
A resource has no effect at the surface until mining disturbs it
A resource can change the soil chemistry and so the vegetation above it
questions.explanation: Metals dispersed from a deposit into the soil can be toxic to some plants and tolerated by others, so the plant community changes. Mapping such changes, sometimes from satellite images, is a way of finding deposits.

questions.stem: A creek draining an unmined area has naturally low pH and high dissolved iron and zinc. Which explanation is best supported?
options: Rainwater in the area is acidic because of a nearby coal-fired power station
Fertiliser from farms upstream is releasing zinc and lowering the creek's pH
Salt from a buried salt dome is dissolving and releasing iron and zinc into the creek
Natural weathering of a sulfide deposit upstream is releasing acid and metals
questions.explanation: Sulfide minerals such as pyrite and sphalerite oxidise when exposed to air and water, forming sulfuric acid and releasing metals, even without mining. The scenario says the area is unmined, so a natural deposit is the best-supported source.

questions.stem: Which deposit is best suited to open-cut mining?
options: A large, low-grade ore body close to the surface
A narrow, high-grade vein extending to great depth
A uranium ore in a deep, permeable sandstone aquifer
A small, rich ore pod under hundreds of metres of rock
questions.explanation: Open-cut mining moves large volumes of rock cheaply, so it suits big deposits near the surface where little waste must be removed. Narrow or deep deposits are mined underground, and ore in a permeable aquifer may suit in-situ leaching.

questions.stem: What is the strip ratio of an open-cut mine?
options: The depth of the pit divided by its width at the surface
The amount of ore processed for each tonne of metal sold
The amount of waste rock removed for each tonne of ore
The proportion of metal in each tonne of ore mined
questions.explanation: The strip ratio compares the waste (overburden) removed with the ore recovered. As a pit deepens the strip ratio rises, and at some point underground mining becomes cheaper. The proportion of metal in ore is its grade.

questions.stem: An open-cut mine has followed a steeply dipping ore body down to 400 m. The company plans to continue by underground mining. Which reason best supports this?
options: Underground mining needs no ventilation or ground support at depth
Going deeper would need far more waste removed for each tonne of ore
Underground mining recovers all of the ore, but open-cut recovers none
The ore becomes less valuable with depth, so less of it is needed
questions.explanation: A pit must widen as it deepens to keep its walls stable, so the waste removed for each tonne of ore climbs steeply. For a deep, steep ore body, tunnels and shafts reach the ore with far less waste. Underground mines need ventilation and ground support.

questions.stem: What happens in in-situ leaching (in-situ recovery) of a mineral resource?
options: The ore is heated underground until the metal melts and flows to a well
Explosives break up the ore underground so it can be hauled up a shaft
A solution is pumped through the ore underground to dissolve the metal
The ore is dug out, crushed and soaked in leaching tanks at the surface
questions.explanation: In in-situ leaching, a leaching solution is injected through wells, dissolves the metal from the ore in place, and is pumped back up recovery wells for processing. No ore is dug up. Heap and tank leaching need the ore to be mined first.

questions.stem: Uranium at Beverley and Four Mile in South Australia lies in permeable sand layers sealed above and below by impermeable clay. Why does this suit in-situ leaching?
options: Impermeable clay lets the solution flow quickly to the surface
Solution can flow through the ore while the clay layers confine it
Clay layers absorb the uranium so the solution does not need to
Permeable sand can be dug easily, so it is mined by bulldozers
questions.explanation: In-situ leaching needs ore that the solution can flow through and impermeable layers that keep the solution in the ore zone. A deposit in a permeable aquifer between clay layers provides both.

questions.stem: Which statement fairly compares in-situ leaching with open-cut mining for a suitable deposit?
options: It causes more surface disturbance, but it produces no impacts on groundwater at all
It produces large tailings dams, but it removes the risk of contaminating groundwater
It suits any type of ore body, but it needs far more waste rock removed than open-cut mining
It causes little surface disturbance and no waste rock, but risks groundwater contamination
questions.explanation: No pit, waste rock dumps or tailings are created, so surface impacts are small. The trade-off is that leaching solution is injected into an aquifer, so excursions of solution and changed groundwater chemistry must be monitored. It only suits permeable, confined ore.

questions.stem: How is oil first brought to the surface from many conventional reservoirs?
options: By heating the reservoir rock until the oil boils off
By dissolving the reservoir rock with injected acid
By natural pressure in the reservoir pushing it up the well
By digging it out of the ground in an open-cut mine
questions.explanation: In primary recovery, the pressure of gas, water and rock in the reservoir drives oil into the well and up it. As pressure falls, water or gas is injected to push more oil to the wells.

questions.stem: Why is water injected into some oil reservoirs after production has been running for some years?
options: It dissolves the oil so it can be pumped as a water solution
It cools the reservoir so the oil does not break down into gas
It seals cracks in the cap rock so oil cannot escape from the top of the trap
It keeps up reservoir pressure and pushes more oil towards the wells
questions.explanation: Production lowers reservoir pressure, so less oil flows. Injecting water maintains pressure and sweeps oil towards the producing wells. Oil does not dissolve in water, which is why it can be pushed ahead of it.

questions.stem: Oil trapped in shale cannot flow freely because the rock has very low permeability. How is it usually extracted?
options: The shale is dissolved underground by acid pumped down the well
The shale is left to drain slowly into a nearby sandstone reservoir over time
Horizontal wells are drilled and the rock is hydraulically fractured
Vertical wells are drilled into the crest of an anticline trap
questions.explanation: Horizontal wells run along the shale layer, and fluid pumped in at high pressure fractures the rock so oil can flow to the well. A conventional vertical well into a trap relies on permeable reservoir rock, which shale lacks.

questions.stem: Oil shale contains kerogen that has never been heated enough to form oil. How can oil be obtained from it?
options: The rock is crushed and washed in water to float the oil off the surface
The rock is left in place and pumped dry to lower the pressure on the oil
The rock is mined and heated in a retort to convert the kerogen to oil
The rock is fractured underground so the oil already in it can flow
questions.explanation: Because the kerogen has not passed through the oil window, there is no free oil to release. Heating the rock in a retort, or sometimes underground, does what burial would have done and converts kerogen to oil. Fracturing only helps where oil has already formed.

questions.stem: Thick seams of brown coal lie close to the surface beneath thin overburden. Which extraction method is most likely?
options: Gas wells that pump water out of the seams
In-situ leaching with an acidic solution
Open-cut mining after the overburden is stripped
Underground longwall mining from deep shafts
questions.explanation: Thick seams near the surface are mined most cheaply by removing the thin overburden and digging the coal in an open cut. Longwall mining is used for deeper seams, and coal cannot be leached in place.

questions.stem: How is coal-seam gas released from a coal seam?
options: Acid is injected to dissolve the coal so the methane is freed into the well
Water is pumped out to lower the pressure, so methane desorbs from the coal
The coal is mined and burnt at the surface, releasing methane from the ash
Steam is injected to melt the coal so the methane bubbles out of the liquid
questions.explanation: Methane is held on coal surfaces by water pressure. Pumping water from the seam lowers the pressure, so the gas is released and flows to the well. This is why coal-seam gas wells produce large volumes of water.

questions.stem: Pyrite (FeS2) in waste rock at a mine is exposed to air and rain. What is the main environmental risk?
options: Radioactive dust that drifts from the waste rock onto farmland
Methane gas that builds up in the waste rock and catches fire
Salt crystals that form a crust over the soil around the dump
Acid mine drainage that carries dissolved metals into waterways
questions.explanation: Pyrite oxidises in air and water to form sulfuric acid, which dissolves heavy metals from the rock. The acidic, metal-laden water harms aquatic life and makes water unfit for stock or irrigation.

questions.stem: The Brukunga mine in the Adelaide Hills produced pyrite for sulfuric acid for fertiliser until 1972. Why has its water had to be treated with lime for decades since?
options: The lime replaces the fertiliser that is no longer produced at the mine site
Pyrite stops oxidising once mining ends, so lime is only needed for safety
Exposed pyrite keeps oxidising, so acid drainage continues long after mining
The lime neutralises the radioactivity left behind by the uranium in the ore
questions.explanation: Sulfide minerals left exposed in the quarry and waste dumps continue to react with air and water, so acid drainage can go on for decades or longer. Lime neutralises the acid and causes dissolved metals to precipitate before the water reaches Dawesley Creek.

questions.stem: Smelting sulfide ores such as galena and chalcopyrite releases a gas that can form acid rain unless it is captured. Which gas?
options: Sulfur dioxide
Carbon monoxide
Methane
Nitrogen
questions.explanation: Heating sulfide ores in air oxidises the sulfur to sulfur dioxide, which forms sulfuric acid in the atmosphere. Many smelters capture it to make sulfuric acid. Methane and nitrogen do not cause acid rain.

questions.stem: Why must tailings from ore processing be stored in engineered dams that are monitored for decades?
options: They are valuable ores that would be stolen if left unprotected
They are pure water that would evaporate if not covered over
They are fine wastes that can hold toxic chemicals and leak or fail
They are coarse boulders that can roll downhill if not contained
questions.explanation: Tailings are finely ground rock left after the valuable mineral is removed, often with processing chemicals and sulfides. Leaks can contaminate groundwater, and dam failures have released toxic slurry over large areas.

questions.stem: Above a coal seam mined by longwall methods, farmland has sunk and creek beds have cracked. What caused this?
options: Shrinking of the soil as the coal dust dried out the land
Subsidence as the rock above the mined-out seam collapsed
Erosion by water pumped out of the mine onto the surface
Earthquakes caused by heat released from the burning coal
questions.explanation: In longwall mining the whole seam is removed and the roof is allowed to collapse behind the machine, so the ground above can sag. Subsidence can crack creek beds and drain surface water into the rocks below.

questions.stem: A coal-seam gas field pumps large volumes of salty water from coal seams. Which pair of impacts must be managed?
options: Disposal of the saline produced water, and lowered water levels in nearby aquifers
Radioactive waste from the gas, and acid rain from burning the produced water
Collapse of the land into open pits, and dust storms from the gas wells
Spread of tailings from the gas, and heating of rivers by the pumped water
questions.explanation: Produced water is often salty and must be treated or stored safely, and pumping it out can lower water levels in connected aquifers used by farmers. Coal-seam gas does not create open pits or tailings.

questions.stem: Methane leaking from gas wells and pipelines is called a fugitive emission. Why is it an environmental concern?
options: Methane destroys the ozone layer in the stratosphere as quickly as CFCs did
Methane is heavier than air, so it collects and smothers crops
Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas, much stronger than CO2 per tonne
Methane reacts with water vapour in the air and falls as acid rain
questions.explanation: Over a century, a tonne of methane traps far more heat than a tonne of carbon dioxide, so leaks add to the enhanced greenhouse effect. Methane does not form acid rain, is not a major ozone-depleting gas and is lighter than air.

questions.stem: A region compares generating electricity from coal and from uranium. Which comparison of their environmental impacts is correct?
options: Neither has impacts on water, because both fuels are burnt in sealed power stations
Coal releases large amounts of CO2; uranium produces small volumes of long-lived radioactive waste
Coal produces long-lived radioactive waste; uranium releases large amounts of CO2 when burnt
Both release large amounts of CO2, but only uranium mining produces any waste rock
questions.explanation: Burning coal releases carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide and ash. Nuclear fission releases no CO2 during generation but produces small volumes of highly radioactive waste that must be isolated for a very long time. Both fuels are mined, so both produce waste rock.
